At the Saturday fair in Rajgarh, Jyoti had told her mother she was at tuition. Now her cousin Mahima was standing at the bangle stall, looking right at her.
"Jyoti? Aren't you supposed to be at Sharma sir's?"
Jyoti's face went hot. "Tuition got cancelled. Sir had a wedding."
"I just saw Sharma sir at the tea stall. He said class was on."
"He's lying. He always forgets." The words tumbled out. "And why are you spying on me? You're always trying to get me in trouble, didi!"
Mahima blinked. "I'm not spying. I came for bangles."
Jyoti turned and walked fast through the crowd, heart thumping, the lie getting heavier with every step. By the time she reached the Ferris wheel she wanted to cry. She had called her favourite teacher a liar and her favourite cousin a spy, all to avoid saying one true sentence.

qa.q: What had Jyoti told her mother about Saturday?
qa.a: Jyoti had told her mother she was at tuition.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti call Mahima a spy?
qa.a: Jyoti panicked and felt ashamed at being caught, so attacking Mahima felt easier than admitting the truth.

qa.q: What could Jyoti do now to stop the lies piling up?
qa.a: Go back to Mahima, admit she skipped tuition, apologise for calling her a spy, and tell her mother herself that evening.

qa.q: How might Mahima feel after being called a spy?
qa.a: Mahima was confused and probably hurt, since she had only come for bangles and was suddenly treated as an enemy.

grounding: Shows a teenager caught in a lie adding new lies and attacking the cousin who found out, because shame makes escape feel easier than admission.

In the family's flat in Amman, Layla opened the shared laptop to print her CV and found Omar's science project folder. Empty. Due tomorrow.
"Omar," she called. "Didn't you tell Mama you finished the project on Tuesday?"
He appeared in the doorway, too fast. "I did. The file got deleted."
"Deleted how?"
"The laptop crashed. Or... you probably deleted it when you were printing all your stuff."
Layla folded her arms. "I haven't printed anything since Sunday."
"Then someone else did. Why are you always checking my things?"
His ears were bright red. His voice had gone high, the way it did when he was little and swore he hadn't eaten the dates.
Layla didn't shout. She just said, "Omar, it's okay to be behind. It's not okay to blame me."
He stood there, mouth open, a third lie ready, and suddenly too tired to say it.

qa.q: What did Layla find in Omar's project folder?
qa.a: The folder was empty, and the project was due tomorrow.

qa.a: They suggest Omar felt panicked and ashamed, grabbing for new lies instead of admitting he hadn't done it.

In the Class 11 staffroom, Ritu ma'am laid two English essays side by side. The same three unusual phrases, the same spelling mistake in "necessary".
"Zainab, can you explain this?"
Zainab's throat closed. She had copied the last two paragraphs from Farah's notebook at 7 am on the bus. "Farah copied from me," she said.
"Farah submitted hers yesterday. Yours came in today."
"Then... I wrote it first in rough. She saw it at lunch." Zainab heard her own voice getting louder. "You always believe her because she's a topper!"
Ritu ma'am didn't raise her voice. "I'm not calling anyone a cheat yet. I'm asking what happened."
The fan clicked above them. Zainab stared at the misspelt word. Each new story needed another to hold it up, and she could feel the whole pile wobbling.
"Can I... sit down?" she whispered.

In Mr Ruiz's history class in Seville, Amara raised her hand. "You wrote 'great analysis of the harbour' on my essay. But my essay was about the railway."
A few students giggled. Mr Ruiz's face went pink. For a second he looked ready to say he'd meant it generally.
Instead he put the stack of papers down. "You're right, Amara. I skimmed several essays too fast last weekend, and I wrote a comment that wasn't about yours. That was careless, and it wasn't honest to hand it back as if I'd read it properly."
The room went quiet. Amara had expected him to get annoyed.
"I'll reread yours tonight and write real comments," he said. "And anyone else who thinks I got theirs wrong, bring it to me. No trouble."
Three students came up after class. Amara noticed she wasn't angry anymore. She was, oddly, a little proud of him.

qa.a: Amara's essay was about the railway.

At the boarding school in Kalimpong, the hostel TV room had been locked for a week. "Wiring problem," Himani ma'am, the warden, had told the Class 10 boys.
On Friday evening Tenzin passed the room and saw the warden inside, watching the news, the TV working perfectly.
He knocked. "Ma'am, is the wiring fixed?"
Himani ma'am froze, remote in hand. Then she sighed and switched off the TV.
"There was no wiring problem, Tenzin. The boys were staying up past lights-out and I didn't want an argument, so I made an excuse. That was a lie, and I'm sorry."
Tenzin had braced for a scolding. Instead he felt strangely grown-up.
"Could you just tell us the real rule?"
"Yes. From tomorrow, TV till nine, and I'll explain why at dinner."
At dinner she did. A few boys grumbled. Nobody sneaked back in after nine that week.

I told Hafsa the truth today, before the library email could.
Two weeks ago she asked if I'd returned her statistics book, and I said yes. I hadn't. I'd left it on the bus and was too embarrassed to say. Every day since, I've jumped whenever her phone buzzed.

I feel awful and lighter at the same time. Mostly lighter.

The milk cooperative office outside Anand smelled of diesel and wet steel cans. Ayesha, twenty, had kept its register for three months. On Monday she'd overslept, missed the early collection from two farms, and written the usual numbers anyway, so nobody would ask.
All night the lie sat on her chest. Those farmers would be paid for milk that had gone sour in their own sheds, and the tanker figures wouldn't match.
At 7 am on Tuesday, before the tanker report arrived, she knocked on the secretary's door. "Akash bhai, I wrote false numbers for Monday. I missed two farms and covered it up."
Akash put down his tea. He was silent a long time. "You'll correct the register in front of me. And you'll go to both farms and explain yourself. No pay for this week."
"Yes."
By noon her feet ached and one farmer had shouted at her. But the register was right. Walking home, she felt ashamed and strangely clean.

I joined, and I brought in my cousins. For eight months everything looked perfect: receipts, small payouts, tea at his house.

The power had gone out at nine, and Suraj sat in the dark flat with rent due at noon the next day. Manoj's side of the room was empty. So was his cupboard.
For seven months Manoj had said he worked at a bank in Andheri. He'd shown Suraj an ID card, talked about his manager, and borrowed money "till salary day" four times. Tonight Manoj's cousin had called: there was no bank job. There had never been.
Suraj went over it again and again by torchlight. The ID card. The stories. Every time he'd lent money, a small voice had said something was off, and every time he'd ignored it. How could he, an accountant, not see it?
At midnight he called his sister. She listened, then said, "Someone who can lie to your face for seven months without blinking is practised. You trusted a friend. That's not the stupid part."
Suraj didn't feel better yet. But he stopped saying "idiot" out loud.

qa.a: Suraj felt foolish and ashamed, replaying every sign and doubting his own judgement as an accountant.

In her PG room in Bengaluru, Bhavna read the message from the cyber cell again. The "Karthik" she had talked to every night for five months, who said he was a naval officer posted at sea, didn't exist. The photos belonged to a fitness trainer in another state. The voice notes came from a number linked to eleven other complaints.
She had never sent him money. He had asked once, for a "medical emergency", and something had made her say no. Still, she felt sick. She had told him about her father's illness, her fears, her salary.
"How did I not see it?" she said to her roommate, Asha.
Asha sat down beside her. "He's done this eleven times, Bhavna. He practises. He's good at it. You were being kind to someone you thought was lonely."
Bhavna laughed, a small cracked sound. She deleted the chat. Then she opened it again, took screenshots of everything for the cyber cell, and deleted it for real.
